title: Accelerating Satellite Conjunction Assessment: Spatial Partitioning and Parallel Computing for Full‐Catalog Collision Screening
content: There are now tens of thousands of tracked objects in orbit, and someone has to check them all for near-misses. The simple way compares every object with every other one, which scales as O(N²). For the 15,830 active objects we look at here, that's over 125 million checks per snapshot—far too many to repeat around the clock. This paper builds and benchmarks a Python pipeline that does the job faster using two ideas from high performance computing: spatial partitioning and parallel processing. We pulled real two-line element data from CelesTrak and propagated it with SGP4. On the full catalog, grid and k-d tree methods checked about 61× fewer pairs than brute force—and found the same 211 close pairs, with zero disagreement. A 24-hour time-window screen picked up real conjunctions and, as a sanity check, correctly flagged co-located structures like the ISS modules and the TanDEM-X/TerraSAR-X formation. Parallelizing the real workload gave a 3.7× speedup on four cores at over 92% efficiency; past that, overhead took over, just as Amdahl's law predicts. Detections stayed identical across every core count, so the parallel version is provably correct. We also estimate each pair's probability of collision, and the headline is simple: the riskiest pair isn't the closest one. Finally we added time-of-closest-approach refinement, a red/yellow/green triage, single-asset screening, and a screen against real debris from the Fengyun-1C, Iridium-33, and Cosmos-1408 break-ups—which turned up a working Starlink satellite passing within 4.4 km of 2009 collision debris.
